To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
incidence of hepatocellular cancer (HCC) did not increase from 1989-2000.
the incidence and mortality of HCC in The Netherlands did not rise, whereas treatment patterns remained stable.
the incidence of HCC did not increase, whereas the number of deaths due to liver cancer did increase.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the incidence and treatment of HCC.
the epidemiology of HCC in a well-defined population in the Western World.
the incidence and treatment pattern of HCC in an unselected population of the Netherlands.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the incidence of HCC has not increased in the Western world and is stable, whereas mortality has increased.
HCC is still a disease that is not diagnosed early enough, is still not treated in a curative way and is still associated with a poor prognosis.
HCC in the Western world is not a rising epidemic.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the incidence of HCC did not increase, but the number of patients receiving no therapy remained high.
the incidence of HCC did not increase in the Netherlands from 1989-2000 and that the treatment of patients with HOC was not optimised.
the treatment of HCC in a Western population is suboptimal and should be improved.
The main takeaway from our work is that
HCC is a disease that is increasing in incidence and mortality in the elderly.
HCC in the Western world is still a disease of elderly men.
there is a significant increase in the incidence of HCC among men older than 65 years.
